text: Assessment of natural mixed infection of turnip mosaic virus and cucumber mosaic virus on growth and yield of mustard genotypes
Pankhuri Singhal1 · Ronit Jaiswal2 · Ashwini Sakpal3 · Malyaj R. Prajapati4 · Virendra Kumar Baranwal1 · Sangita Yadav3 · Jitender Singh5
Received: 15 May 2024 / Accepted: 6 March 2025 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Deutsche Phytomedizinische Gesellschaft 2025

Cucumoviruses and potyviruses are the most destructive viruses of crop plants. In the experimental mustard field of IARI, New Delhi, in 2021 eight genotypes were observed with mosaic, puckering, and stunting symptoms. The next-generation sequencing (NGS) confirmed the infection of two viruses, i.e., turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) and cucumber mosaic virus (CMV), validated through reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR). In the following year, i.e., 2022, the same genotypes showed only puckering symptoms on the leaves with slight stunting. The association of only TuMV was found via NGS and RT-PCR. A study was undertaken to evaluate the impact of natural mixed infection of TuMV and CMV on the growth and yield of mustard genotypes and compared the same with the impact of natural infection of TuMV alone. The variance analysis results from data collected on various growth parameters, such as plant height and main shoot length, were significant, with mixed infections of TuMV and CMV causing severe stunting. The yield parameters, including the number of seeds per siliqua and the test weight of 1000 seeds, were significantly lower under mixed infection conditions than with TuMV alone. The coinfections have a substantial effect on the seed yield per plant with reduction factor of 2.5–4 across different genotypes compared to single TuMV infections. However, the reduction in oil content was minimal and less significant. This study provides the first comprehensive analysis of the effects of TuMV and CMV mixed infections on mustard growth and yield compared to single infection of TuMV, highlighting the highly negative impact of mixed infections on crop productivity. These findings underscore the need for integrated virus management strategies in mustard cultivation.
Keywords Mixed infection · Turnip mosaic virus · Cucumber mosaic virus · Mosaic · Puckering
1 Division of Plant Pathology, ICAR-Indian Agricultural

Mustard, an annual member of the Brassicaceae family, is India’s second most important oilseed crop, following soy- bean. In addition to being a primary source of edible oil, mustard serves as a condiment and a source of vegetable leaves, making it a versatile crop. Three main types of mus- tard are cultivated globally: brown mustard, often referred to as Indian mustard (Brassica juncea); black mustard (B. nigra), believed to have originated in Asia Minor or Iran; and yellow mustard (Brassica rapa subsp. trilocularis), which likely originated in the Mediterranean region.

The number of viruses linked with plants in both natural and man-made ecosystems is extremely diverse, with each virus’s biological, epidemiological, and socioeconomic rel- evance varying. Mixed viral infections can occur frequently and can result in complex interactions between viruses and
their hosts, often exacerbating disease severity (Singhal et al.

2021). Among these, cucumber mosaic virus (CMV) and turnip mosaic virus (TuMV) are considered among the most widespread viruses (Tomlinson 1987). Synergistic effects between these viruses and their co-infecting counterparts are frequently observed, leading to heightened symptom sever- ity and increased virus titers in host plants. In a previous study in radish (Raphanus sativus L.), single infections of TuMV induced mild symptoms, while mixed infections with CMV caused severe mosaic symptoms, accompanied by elevated CMV titers (Sano and Kojima 1989). Similarly, in Nicotiana benthamiana, combined CMV and TuMV infec- tions produced more severe symptoms than single infec- tions (Takeshita et al. 2012). The mixed infection of TuMV with other viruses, such as ribgrass mosaic virus (RMV), has been shown to significantly increase disease severity, with co-infection rates as high as 31.9% compared to 13.9% and 4.5% in RMV and TuMV single infections, respectively (Yoon et al. 1995). In Brassica crops, TuMV alone has been reported to cause yield losses of up to 70% (Nellist et al. 2022), with a reduction of up to 70% in seed yield in B. napus (Hardwick et al. 1994) and a 50% decrease in head
production in B. oleracea (Spence et al. 2007).

Earlier, the impact of mixed infections of CMV and TuMV has been studied in winter oilseed rape in experi- mental settings (Spak and Novikov 1994). The effects of mixed infections in naturally cultivated mustard genotypes, however, remain unexplored. At the experimental fields at the Indian Council of Agricultural Research—Indian Agri- cultural Research Institute (ICAR- IARI), New Delhi, mixed infections of two viruses, i.e., TuMV and CMV as well as a single infection of TuMV, were confirmed by next-genera- tion sequencing (NGS) and Sanger sequencing of RT-PCR amplicons (Singhal et al. 2022, 2023). To address the knowl- edge gap, a comprehensive study was conducted to evaluate the agronomic and yield parameters, including oil content across different mustard genotypes. This study aimed to analyze the individual and combined impacts of mixed and single infections by collective data analysis, providing criti- cal insights into the differential effects of these infections on mustard productivity.

The seeds of eight genotypes obtained from seed stock at IARI, New Delhi, were used for sowing in a randomized block design with three replications. The details of the genotypes used in the experiment are provided in Table 1. Fifty uniformly sized seeds from each of the eight genotypes for each replication were sown in the 3rd and 4th week of

The symptomatic leaf samples from mustard plants of the same genotypes of both years were collected and subjected to an electron microscopy (EM) analysis using the standard methodology of leaf dip method in 2 percent aqueous uranyl acetate (UA). Furthermore, pooled leaf samples of all eight genotypes were used for RNA isolation according to the Qia- gen RNeasy Plant Mini Kit instructions, and samples of two same genotypes from each year were subjected to virome analysis via the high-throughput (HTS) RNA-seq approach. The quantity and quality of the RNA were assessed using a NanoDropTM spectrophotometer (ThermoScientific, Wilm-

The methodology adopted for HTS and raw data analy- sis in both years have been previously published (Singhal et al. 2022, 2023). The genomic area coding for replicase was the sole region taken into consideration for estimation of the copy number (Fragments per Kilobase of transcripts per Million mapped reads—FPKM) of viruses, excluding the regions encoding subgenomic RNAs (sgRNA). The viral genome sequences isolated from the relevant cultivars were used for mapping the trimmed reads individually using CLC workbench with default parameters (similarity fraction—0.8; length fraction—0.5). The virome analysis results were vali- dated through RT-PCR assays followed by Sanger sequenc- ing of the amplicons (Singhal et al. 2022, 2023).

Statistical analyses were conducted separately for each experimental year, followed by a combined analysis of the two-year dataset. The analysis involved the following

• Individual Year Analysis: Initial analysis was per- formed for each year separately to examine the effects of the treatments on agronomic and yield parameters within that year’s unique environmental and infection

• Homogeneity of Variance Test: Before combining the datasets, Bartlett’s Chi-square test was applied to assess the homogeneity of error variances across the two years. This step was crucial to determine whether data from different years could be analyzed together
• Homogeneous Variances: If Bartlett’s test indicated homogeneous error variances, the data from both years were combined, treating each year as an additional factor
in a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA).

• Heterogeneous Variances: If the error variances were heterogeneous, an adjustment was applied to stabilize variance across years. Aitken’s transformation, in which each observation is divided by the root-mean-square error of the respective year, was utilized as a straight- forward method of data normalization. The transformed
data were then used for further analysis.

• Combined Analysis and Treatment-Years Interaction: Following verification of homogeneity, combined analy- sis was conducted using two-way ANOVA, with "Year" as an additional factor to account for any year-specific
• Interaction Check: The interaction between treatments (genotypes) and years was tested to evaluate whether the treatment effects differed significantly across the two years.
– If the treatment × year interaction was significant, the treatment effects were compared with the mean square
of the interaction to interpret significant differences.
– If the interaction was non-significant, treatment effects were evaluated against the pooled mean square of the
combined treatment × year interaction and error term.

The results revealed distinct symptomatology in mustard plants depending on the type of viral infection. Symptoms in plants with single infections of TuMV were noticed early due to seed transmission, exhibiting severe puckering on the leaves without any mosaic patterns and only slight stunting of the plants (Fig. 2). In contrast, plants co-infected with CMV, likely introduced through aphid transmission at later stages of growth, displayed symptoms that differed signifi- cantly. Puckering became less pronounced, while the leaves

developed a severe mosaic pattern characterized by light and dark green areas. These co-infected plants also exhibited severe stunting compared to those infected with TuMV alone (Figs. 1 and 2). As indicated by the field images, quality mustard genotypes were more stunted as compared to the conventional genotype and single zero types especially when
subjected to mixed infection of both viruses.

of seeds per siliqua, seed yield per plant, test weight, and oil content. The combined ANOVA across both years revealed key effects related to infection types. The year effect was highly significant (p < 0.0001), confirming substantial differences in plant height between the years with mixed and single infections, likely due to the differential impacts of viral stress. The treatment (genotype) effect also remained highly significant (p < 0.0001) in the combined analysis, reinforcing the presence of genetic differences in plant height across the study period. Additionally, the significant replication within year interaction (p = 0.010) suggests that block effects varied across years, possibly due to differing infection conditions. The significant treatment within year interaction (p = 0.011) indicates that genotype performance differed between years, which could reflect genotype-specific responses to the com- bined stress of TuMV and CMV versus single-virus infec- tion. The residual mean square in the combined analysis was 145, which reflects the general level of within-genotype vari- ability across both years. Tukey’s pairwise comparison in the combined analysis supported similar findings to the first ANOVA, with PDZ-5 remaining the most severely stunted

Mixed viral infections led to a substantial reduction in main shoot length, with the average shoot length across geno- types measuring 36.5 cm. In contrast, plants with infection of TuMV alone showed a much smaller reduction, with an average shoot length of 50 cm. Utilizing growth indicators including plant height, weight, yield, and effects on seeds, it has been possible to deter- mine the synergism caused by mixed virus infection (Win- termantel 2005; Pio-Ribeiro et al. 1978). In response to mixed infection, there has been a noticeable decrease in growth characteristics (i.e., quantitative parameters). How- ever, assessments of the severity of symptoms have mostly remained descriptive, lacking a statistical foundation for the occurrence of synergy. Oilseed rape and mustard are known to be hosts for more than 12 viruses, and they may occur in mixed infections, causing significant economic losses. Although mosaic disease of mustard has mostly been attrib- uted to TuMV, mixed infections of TuMV and CMV have been reported in a few cases (Sano and Kojima 1989). In another study, high rates of mixed infections of two or more viruses, i.e., TuMV, CMV, and BrYV, have been reported in China (Zhang et al. 2022). After plants are simultaneously infected with potyviruses, CMV has been shown to alter the host’s intrinsic metabolism and worsen disease severity (Wang et al. 2002a, b). A synergistic relationship results in greater virus replication in the host plant and has a facilita- tive influence on both viral partners or on at least one of

This study provides an in-depth assessment of the effects of single and mixed infections of TuMV and CMV on the growth, yield, and oil content of mustard under natural field conditions through collective data analysis on eight mustard genotypes, including conventional and biofortified varieties. The HTS RNA-seq approach, along with Sanger sequencing of RT-PCR amplicons, was used to demonstrate the presence of CMV + TuMV in the 2020–2021 mustard genotypes and only TuMV in 2021–2022 mustard genotypes. The viral titer of TuMV was observed to be higher in single infections of mustard genotypes than in mixed infections as revealed by the copy number generated via reference-based mapping of the viral reads. The difference in infection could be due to seed-borne infection by TuMV (Singhal et al. 2024) and only aphid transmission of CMV, which might have come in the first year from some nearby infected source. The difference

in time of infection leads to differential symptom expression. Symptom studies revealed that single infections of TuMV caused only puckering and slight stunting, while mixed infections with CMV induced more severe mosaic symp- toms, leaf distortion, and significant stunting. The seed- borne nature of TuMV facilitated early infections, while CMV, transmitted via aphids, appeared later, intensifying disease severity. This sequential infection likely exacer- bated the detrimental effects on growth and yield param- eters. The mosaic symptoms observed in mixed infections were consistent with findings in other studies where CMV and potyviruses interact synergistically to amplify symptom severity (Sano & Kojima 1989; Fattouh 2003). In another study, the mixed infections of TuMV with potato virus X (PVX) and potato virus Y (PVY) have been reported to pro- duce severe veinal necrosis compared to single infections of TuMV, which cause only mild mottle or vein banding

The synergism caused by mixed infections of CMV and TuMV was evident in the significant reductions observed in plant height, main shoot length, and branch density. Mixed infections caused more severe stunting compared to single infections of TuMV, with double-zero mustard genotypes exhibiting the most pronounced reductions. This aligns with previous studies where mixed infections of potyviruses and cucumoviruses have led to greater reductions in growth traits than single infections alone (Wang et al. 2002a, b; Murphy and Bowen 2006). The inverse effect observed on branch numbers suggests that severe reductions in height and main shoot length caused a compensatory bushy appearance, par- ticularly under mixed infection stress.

Yield-related traits, including siliqua density, seeds per siliqua, test weight, and seed yield per plant, were signifi- cantly compromised by mixed infections. Mixed infections resulted in a siliqua density of 0.97 compared to 0.55 for TuMV single infections, demonstrating a stark reduction in reproductive potential. The 1000-seed weight also decreased considerably in mixed infections, reflecting compromised seed quality. Seed yield per plant under mixed infections was reduced by more than three times compared to single infections, underscoring the compounded negative effects of CMV and TuMV interactions. These findings resonate with earlier reports on synergistic interactions between CMV and other viruses like pepper mottle virus (PepMoV) and bean common mosaic virus (BCMV), which caused signifi- cant yield losses in their respective hosts (Pio-Ribeiro et al. 1978; Murphy & Bowen 2006). Although oil content was slightly reduced in mixed infections, the difference was not as substantial as the impact on other yield parameters. This observation suggests that oil biosynthesis pathways may be relatively less affected compared to the physiological pro- cesses underlying growth and reproduction under mixed
The synergistic interactions between CMV and TuMV in

mustard plants carry significant epidemiological implica- tions. The enhanced disease severity and yield reductions observed in mixed infections highlight the potential for increased economic losses in mustard cultivation. Similar interactions reported in other crops, such as cowpea and oriental cabbage, underscore the importance of managing mixed infections (Pio-Ribeiro et al. 1978; Kim et al. 2003, 2010). This exaggerated effect of the viruses in mixed as well as single infections in the November sown crops could be due to severe virus infestation as well as the secondary spread of viruses by the aphid vectors that play a significant role in enhanced disease severity. It was also difficult to sep- arate CMV on differential hosts in this study too, as reported previously (Sano and Kojima 1989). Therefore, the effects of single infections of CMV on growth and yield parameters could not be analyzed. The mixed infections of cucumovirus with a potyvirus are often considered detrimental, leading to severe yield reductions (Wang et al. 2002a, b; Choi et al. 2002; Barbosa et al. 2016). In other report of CMV, mixed infections with BCMV cause cowpea stunt disease in the mid-eastern USA, leading to yield losses of up to 84% as compared with 14.2% and 2.5% caused by single infections of CMV and BCMV, respectively (Pio-Ribeiro et al. 1978). Similarly, mixed infections of CMV along with zucchini Yellow Mosaic Virus (ZYMV) of squash (Cucurbita pepo) resulted in a synergistic effect with enhanced symptoms and disease severity (Fattouh 2003). Instead of being mediated by the replication of genomic RNA, potyviral synergism with other homologous viruses is mediated by the expres- sion of specific sequences in the 5’ proximal one-third of the genome (Vance 1991). This study is the first to quantify the effects of single and mixed infections of CMV and TuMV on mustard genotypes under natural field conditions. The findings emphasize the critical need for integrated disease management strategies to prevent mixed infections, which pose a severe threat to mustard production. Strategies such as using resistant gen- otypes, controlling aphid vectors, and ensuring virus-free seeds should be prioritized to mitigate the risks associated with mixed infections. These efforts will help safeguard mustard crops from the compounded effects of viral syner- gism, ensuring sustainable production and economic stabil- ity for farmers.
